title: Natural Vegetation, Forests, Wildlife and Biodiversity
intake_rule: Each printed page was visually read once from its rendered image. Handwriting was ignored. Printed claims are preserved here before scientific correction; dynamic statistics are dated.
table_policy: Every printed table is reproduced cell-by-cell in notes, followed by a clearly labelled correction or current-data table where needed. Concepts are explained in prose; comparisons and datasets use responsive semantic tables.

facts.claim: ISFR 2023 forest cover is 715,342.61 km² or 21.76% of India; tree cover is 112,014.34 km² or 3.41%; together they are 827,356.95 km² or 25.17%.
Very Dense Forest has canopy density at least 70%; Moderately Dense Forest 40-70%; Open Forest 10-40%; scrub is below the forest-cover threshold.
FSI has conducted nationwide biennial forest-resource assessment since 1987; sensor resolution and interpretation methods have changed over time.
State rankings by absolute forest area and by forest percentage answer different questions and must not be interchanged.
State leadership differs among forest cover, tree cover, scrub, bamboo-bearing area and growing stock because each indicator measures a different resource.
Global forest distribution must be tied to the named FAO assessment and its regional definitions.
ISFR state/UT area tables require units, edition and separate treatment of states and union territories.
Mizoram and several north-eastern states have high forest-cover percentages, while Madhya Pradesh leads by absolute forest-cover area.
ISFR 2023 estimated India's forest carbon stock at 7,285.5 million tonnes, an increase over the 2021 assessment.
The National Forest Policies of 1952 and 1988 share the one-third land-area aspiration but differ in emphasis; draft policy documents are not enacted policy.

facts.claim: FRA 2025 reports forest area by country and forest share of land area as different indicators.
The Russian Federation, Brazil, Canada, United States and China together hold more than half of global forest area in FRA 2025.
Champion and Seth classify Indian forests using ecological conditions and floristic composition; broad exam groups must not erase subtypes.
Tropical evergreen forest develops under persistently warm, very wet conditions and forms a multi-storeyed closed canopy with no common leaf-fall season.
Semi-evergreen forest is a transition in which evergreen and moist-deciduous elements occur together.
Shola is a montane forest-grassland mosaic of the higher southern Western Ghats, not simply any evergreen forest at altitude.
Moist deciduous forests occupy wetter monsoonal regions and commonly include sal or teak depending on region and substrate.
Dry deciduous forests occur under a longer dry season and more open canopy than moist deciduous forests.
Rainfall, dry-season length, altitude, soil and disturbance together explain forest distribution; a single rainfall cutoff is an exam approximation.
The printed APPSC Group-II 2024 question identifies tropical dry deciduous forest as India's most extensive forest type.
Thorn forest has drought-adapted plants with reduced leaves, thorns, deep roots or water-storing tissues.
Desert scrub is sparser and more xeric than thorn forest; subtropical montane forest reflects elevation-driven cooling and moisture.
Himalayan forest belts change with altitude, aspect and moisture from subtropical through temperate to subalpine and alpine vegetation.
Himalayan dry temperate forest occurs mainly in rain-shadow or drier inner valleys and differs from moist temperate forest in canopy and species composition.
The climatic treeline separates closed forest from subalpine scrub and alpine meadow; its elevation varies locally.

facts.claim: Mangroves are salt-tolerant intertidal woody communities; pneumatophores aid gas exchange in waterlogged anoxic sediment and vivipary helps establishment.
ISFR 2023 records 4,991.68 km² of mangrove cover, 7.43 km² below the revised 2021 raster assessment.
The printed Odisha row is internally inconsistent; official ISFR 2023 gives 259.06 km² and a +1.55 km² change.
AP mangrove cover in ISFR 2023 is 421.43 km², with Krishna district largest at 148.45 km².
The printed district table duplicates Nellore and omits Eluru; the official table lists SPSR Nellore once and Eluru at 0.02 km².
Country share rankings and species-richness rankings describe different aspects of world mangroves and must be dated and sourced separately.

tables: AP district mangrove cover and change

facts.claim: Reserved, protected and unclassed forests are legal-status categories; they are not canopy-density classes.
Forest species provide timber, oils, food, fibre, medicines and cultural products; a species-use association does not imply exclusive occurrence in one forest type.

tables: important trees and uses part I

facts.claim: Deodar, chir pine, cane, tendu, mahua, semal, grasses, gums, tannins, dyes and lac have distinct ecological distributions and uses.
Grassland within a forest assessment is not the same as forest cover; quoted percentages require the source classification and denominator.

tables: important trees and uses part II

facts.claim: Indian Forest Act 1927, Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and Biological Diversity Act 2002 have different purposes.
Project Tiger began in 1973; social forestry expanded through programmes in the early 1980s; Van Mahotsav has been observed annually since 1950.
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List and inserted Articles 48A and 51A(g).
The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 reorganised schedules; CITES appendices and Indian statutory schedules are different legal classifications.
Social forestry includes farm, community and extension/urban forms whose ownership, site and beneficiaries differ.
The ISFR 2023 thematic map represents forest-cover density classes, not legal forest ownership or a list of forest types.
Map colours must be decoded through the legend before making comparisons; apparent area on a small-scale map is not a substitute for tabulated measurement.
India's wildlife conservation institutions developed through colonial species laws, the Indian Forest Act, post-Independence wildlife policy and the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.

Hailey National Park, notified in 1936 and later renamed Jim Corbett National Park, is India's first national park; Vedanthangal has an older community/protection history but category and notification dates must be stated carefully.
Project Tiger began in 1973 with nine reserves and is now administered through NTCA under the Wildlife (Protection) Act framework.

facts.claim: The printed state-wise tiger-reserve list contains obsolete names, omissions and non-reserve protected areas; the current NTCA list has 58 reserves in 18 states.

Kudremukh and Dinosaur Fossil National Park are not tiger reserves; Karnataka's current tiger reserves include Biligiri Ranganatha and Kali, while Madhya Pradesh includes Veerangana Durgavati, Ratapani and Madhav.
Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam is Andhra Pradesh's tiger reserve; Amrabad and Kawal are in Telangana.
Indian tiger estimation moved beyond pugmark-only counting to camera traps, field signs, spatial analysis and M-STrIPES-supported monitoring.
All-India tiger estimates for 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022 belong to separate estimation cycles and should not be mixed with state minima/maxima or reserve counts.
The Asiatic lion's sole wild population is centred on the Gir landscape of Gujarat; lion conservation and tiger-reserve administration are separate programmes.

tables: tiger population series and state ranking

facts.claim: NTCA is the statutory body for tiger conservation; the International Big Cat Alliance is a separate international initiative launched in 2023.
Melanistic or black tigers show unusually dark striping caused by a colour-pattern variant; they are not a separate tiger species.
India has 106 national parks in the current WII dataset; counts and area must carry a date because notifications change.
A national park, wildlife sanctuary and tiger reserve are different legal or management categories; a site may overlap categories but the names are not interchangeable.
The printed state-wise national-park table must retain each cell but mark entries that are tiger reserves, sanctuaries, fossil parks or renamed sites rather than current national parks.

tables: major national parks by state part I

facts.claim: Keibul Lamjao in Manipur is noted for floating phumdi habitat; Hemis in Ladakh is a high-altitude Trans-Himalayan national park.
Current names and categories must be checked for every park in the continuation table, including Mukundra Hills, Anamalai/Indira Gandhi and Mount Manipur/Mount Harriet.

facts.claim: Natural World Heritage properties, national parks and biosphere reserves are different designations; some sites overlap but one label does not imply the others.
The Western Ghats is a serial UNESCO World Heritage property, not one national park.
A biosphere reserve combines conservation, sustainable development and logistic support through core, buffer and transition arrangements.

tables: UNESCO natural World Heritage protected areas

facts.claim: India has 18 nationally designated biosphere reserves; inclusion in UNESCO's World Network is a separate international recognition.
Cold Desert joined UNESCO's World Network in 2025 as India's thirteenth network site, after the printed list's earlier twelve.
Seshachalam Hills is Andhra Pradesh's nationally designated biosphere reserve but is not in UNESCO's World Network as of this verification.
Project Elephant began in 1992; elephant reserves and elephant population estimates are separate datasets.
Green, yellow and red elephant-conflict zones express increasing conflict risk or management priority, not IUCN threat categories.
Crocodile, musk deer, sea turtle, snow leopard, great Indian bustard, rhino and vulture recovery programmes differ in launch year, geography and implementing institution.
Project Cheetah began with eight cheetahs from Namibia released at Kuno in September 2022; later imports and survival figures are time-sensitive.
Indian fauna distribution follows habitat and biogeographic regions; species lists must distinguish native range, reintroduction site and captive occurrence.
ICFRE institutes specialise by region or research theme; institute name, location and mandate must be matched independently.
The Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981 and Environment (Protection) Act 1986 address different regulatory subjects.
Andhra Pradesh vegetation reflects rainfall, relief, soils, altitude and coastal influence rather than administrative boundaries alone.
AP moist deciduous, dry deciduous and thorn forests form a moisture gradient and differ in canopy, district distribution and dominant species.
The printed AP vegetation map is a thematic generalisation and must be read with its legend and current district boundaries.
AP coastal vegetation includes mangroves in estuaries and deltas; mangrove cover is not distributed uniformly along the entire coast.
ISFR 2023 gives AP mangrove cover as 421.43 km²; older coastline-length figures and rankings must be dated and verified before scoring.
Counts of sanctuaries, national parks, zoos and other conservation facilities describe different categories and must not be totalled as one protected-area count.
The printed AP sanctuary table links each site to district, area and a characteristic species; all four fields require current official review.
Papikonda, Sri Venkateswara and Rajiv Gandhi are the three national parks listed for residual Andhra Pradesh in the book.
Deer parks and zoological parks are not national parks or wildlife sanctuaries and must remain in separate tables.
ISFR 2023 reports AP forest cover of 30,084.96 km² or 18.46%, with a decrease of 138.66 km² from the revised 2021 assessment.
AP district rankings by forest area, percentage forest cover and change are three different rankings.
Seshachalam biosphere reserve, Kaundinya elephant landscape and Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam tiger reserve represent different conservation designations.
Joint/Community Forest Management, afforestation, soil-moisture conservation, CAMPA and Green India Mission differ in legal basis, finance and implementation structure.
Funding ratios and administrative tiers are period-specific; the State FDA, FDA and VSS hierarchy should be learned with programme context.

tables: forestry programme funding and institutional hierarchy

facts.claim: AP forest products include timber and non-timber products such as bamboo, tendu leaves, gums, honey, mahua and medicinal products; red sanders requires special conservation and trade controls.
Kolleru, Pulicat, Nelapattu and other wetlands or sanctuaries have distinct bird assemblages and legal status.
The printed APPSC Group-I 2022 matching question links Coringa, Gundla Brahmeswaram, Rollapadu and Sri Lankamalleswara sanctuaries with characteristic fauna.
Jerdon's courser, slender loris, golden gecko, red sanders and Cycas beddomei represent different animal and plant conservation cases in Andhra Pradesh.
The Great Indian Bustard is a threatened grassland bird recorded historically in AP, but it is not Andhra Pradesh's current state bird.
Endemic means naturally restricted to a defined geographic area; rare, endangered, protected and endemic are not synonyms.
